summary: A 1968 paper on binary message forms in computer networks. It argues that although the content and form of messages between computers cannot easily be standardised, a standard way of describing message forms could help, in the way ALGOL is used to describe algorithms.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 31 proposes a symbolic language for describing binary message formats. It names message fields and explains their order and alternatives before listing how many bits each field uses.

questions: binary message forms in computer networks
how did rfc 31 describe binary messages
what symbols did the message notation use
subtitle: A symbolic method for describing the structure of binary messages.

tldr.problem: Different computers need to exchange binary message bodies, and descriptions that jump straight to bit layouts can obscure their structure.
tldr.mechanism: The paper proposes naming fields and values, describing how fields combine, and declaring field sizes separately.
tldr.outcome: The notation is presented as a way to document message formats so readers can understand their structure before their bit-level coding.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 31 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text presents a method for describing binary message forms and includes a worked picture-data example.

sections.title: Describe the Message Before Its Bits
sections.content:
The authors say that different network installations make standardizing message content and form difficult. They argue that a standard way to describe message forms could still help people understand what data computers exchange.

Rather than starting with boxes of bits, the proposed method describes the symbolic structure first and then gives the coding details. The paper assumes that message exchange mechanics, checksums and repeat requests have already been worked out.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper focuses on explaining what a binary message contains, not how computers send it. It proposes describing the message's structure before listing its bit details.

sections.title: Four Parts of a Format Description
sections.content:
A description has a title and four declarative sections: names for simple fields, names for commonly used field values, statements showing how fields combine, and the bit sizes of simple fields. The paper says field sizes should appear at the end so readers can first understand the message structure.

In the combination statements, + joins fields, / marks alternatives, and = followed by a number indicates repetition. Parentheses group parts of an expression.
sections.plainLanguage: A format description names its pieces, gives names to important values, shows how the pieces fit together and lists each piece's size. Symbols show joining, choices and repetition.

sections.title: Values, Repetition and Conditional Fields
sections.content:
The notation can assign a field's integer value to a variable and use that variable to state how many times a later field repeats. It can also make a field optional based on the value of an earlier field, using a condition and brackets.

The paper also describes alternatives selected by the value of an earlier field. These features let a format description express messages whose later parts depend on earlier values.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can say how many later pieces it contains by giving a count in an earlier field. It can also include or choose later fields based on an earlier value.

sections.title: Example: A Hierarchical Picture Message
sections.content:
The worked example describes pictorial data made from points and lines. It defines fields such as options, coordinates, identifiers and a count, then combines them into larger structures such as points, lines, picture units and a complete picture message.

The example shows how symbolic names can describe nested message structure, while a separate field-size declaration supplies bit widths.
sections.plainLanguage: The example builds a picture message from small named fields and larger groups of fields. The reader can follow the structure before consulting the sizes of the individual fields.
